Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Mara, the venue’s access coordinator, copied the newest export into a separate working folder and wrote the arrival time on the paper checklist. The band had played the room twice before, but this was the first show for which the venue had arranged live captions on the side screens as well as a downloadable subtitle file for the recording.

The recording was a little under ninety minutes long. It included the opening announcement, the full set, and a short conversation between the singer, Lena Ortiz, and the audience near the end. The subtitle file contained 684 cues, with timecodes based on the camera feed rather than the soundboard recording. That difference mattered: the camera audio was about four tenths of a second behind the mix, and the delay changed slightly after the interval. Mara noted both offsets before she started comparing the text with the recording. She did not want the team to mistake a timing issue for a missing line.

1. The first pass

Mara listened from the opening announcement while following each cue on her laptop. The first minute was straightforward. The house manager said, “Welcome to the Harbor Room. Please keep the center aisle clear,” and the caption appeared on both screens before the audience began to applaud. A few cues had been split at natural pauses, which made them easier to read from the back of the room. In one place, however, the file displayed “doors close at half past eight” while the announcement clearly said “doors open at half past eight.” Mara marked the cue for correction and replayed that section twice before moving on.

The band’s first song was called “Paper Satellites,” not “Paper Satellite,” as it appeared in the set list attached to the email. The lyrics were not supplied in advance, so Mara checked the audio rather than trying to fill in uncertain words from the band’s website. Most of the lines were clear, but the mix buried a brief phrase under a cymbal crash. She left the existing wording in place and added a comment for the caption operator to listen again during sound check. In a subtitle file, a confident-looking guess could be harder to notice than an obvious blank, especially when the audience had no other way to check the line.

At 9:03, the caption operator, Dev, called from the control booth. He had noticed that the live display and the recording export disagreed about the song break. The live system showed a short silence after cue 214, while the file ran the singer’s introduction directly into the next song. Mara checked the camera recording and found that the export had trimmed seven seconds of crowd noise. The singer’s introduction was still present, but its first sentence began earlier than the audio actually did. She adjusted the cue boundary to match the recording and sent Dev the new timecode, keeping the longer pause on the live screen so the audience would not see text during the applause.

2. Names, timing, and audience notes

The second pass focused on names and on-screen information. Lena introduced the violinist as “Nico Vale,” while the tour sheet spelled his surname Vail. Dev asked whether the subtitle should follow the spoken introduction or the tour sheet. Mara sent a short message to the band manager, who confirmed that the correct spelling was Vale. The manager also confirmed the name of the guest drummer, Simone Park, whose surname had been omitted from the first export. Mara corrected both names and checked that the changes appeared in the cue list, the plain-text transcript, and the version prepared for the recording.

A separate note from the venue asked that the file identify the two songs performed in the encore. The recording showed the band returning after the lights came up, but the camera did not capture the printed set list. Mara checked the announcement made by the stage manager, then compared it with the titles spoken by Lena before each song. The first was “North Window”; the second was “Small Hours.” She added the titles as brief on-screen cues, not as lyrics, and made sure the cue for “Small Hours” did not cover the interpreter’s hands in the lower corner of the wide shot.

The subtitle file also included audience speech near the front row. A person asked whether the venue would run a late bus after the show, and Lena replied that the box office had a printed schedule. Mara kept the question and answer because they were audible and relevant to the conversation, but she did not add a route number: nobody said one. The venue’s travel page listed two different departure times, and the production team had not asked her to verify them. In her notes, she wrote that the box office schedule should remain visible on the lobby noticeboard until the final audience members had left.

In the final section, Lena thanked the volunteer team and said the Harbor Room had kept a jar of earplugs by the entrance for years. The caption in the file read “a jar of earplugs by the interest,” an error caused by a noisy consonant in the room recording. Mara listened to the isolated channel, checked the same sentence in the live-captions log, and confirmed “entrance.” She repaired the word and then reviewed the whole sentence in context. The brief laugh afterward belonged to the audience, not to Lena, so Mara did not attach it to the spoken line or turn it into a speaker label.

By 10:26, the revised file had passed the timing check on both the camera recording and the soundboard mix. Mara saved it as `harbor_room_concert_access.srt` and moved the earlier exports into an archive folder without deleting them. Dev loaded the new version onto the side-screen system and checked the opening announcement, the two encore titles, and the last spoken cue. Before leaving, Mara wrote the remaining sound-check note beside the cymbal-masked lyric and handed the paper checklist to the morning technician.
